Abstract.

The nn-dimensional lattice polytopes 𝒬n,k\mathcal{Q}_{n,k} obtained by intersecting the nnth dilate of the standard nn-dimensional simplex in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with the half-spaces xi≤1x_{i}\leq 1 for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k form an interesting special case of Chapoton’s arbor polytopes. They interpolate between the nnth dilate of the standard nn-dimensional simplex and the standard nn-dimensional cube in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. This paper provides an explicit combinatorial interpretation of the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial of 𝒬n,k\mathcal{Q}_{n,k}, as the ascent enumerator of certain words, and partly confirms some of Chapoton’s conjectures on the lattice point enumeration of arbor polytopes in this special case. More specifically, the Ehrhart polynomial of 𝒬n,k\mathcal{Q}_{n,k} is shown to be magic positive, by means of a new combinatorial parking model for cars, and the real-rootedness of its h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial is deduced. The polynomial whose coefficients count the lattice points of 𝒬n,k\mathcal{Q}_{n,k} by the number of their nonzero coordinates is shown to be gamma-positive and a combinatorial interpretation of the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial of any arbor polytope is conjectured.

1. Introduction

Given a positive integer nn and k∈{0,1,…,n}k\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}, we will be primarily interested in the polytope 𝒬n,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k} in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} defined by the inequalities

(1)
xi≥0x_{i}\geq 0 for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n,
xi≤1x_{i}\leq 1 for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, and
x1+x2+⋯+xn≤nx_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}\leq n,

where x1,x2,…,xnx_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n} are the standard coordinates of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n}. This nn-dimensional lattice polytope specializes to the nnth dilate of the standard nn-dimensional simplex and to the standard nn-dimensional cube in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} for k=0k=0 and k=nk=n, respectively.

The polytopes 𝒬n,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k} belong to the class of arbor polytopes, introduced and studied by Chapoton [8]. Let us recall their definition. An arbor on the ground set [n]:={1,2,…,n}[n]:=\{1,2,\dots,n\} is a rooted tree with vertices the blocks of a partition of [n][n]. We call nn the size of the arbor. Given such an arbor τ\tau, the polytope 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} is defined by the inequalities xi≥0x_{i}\geq 0 for i∈[n]i\in[n] and

∑i∈𝒟⁡(v)xi≤|𝒟⁡(v)|\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{D}}(v)}x_{i}\leq|{\mathcal{D}}(v)|

for all vertices vv of τ\tau, where 𝒟⁡(v){\mathcal{D}}(v) is the union of all vertices which are descendants of vv in τ\tau (including vv itself). Thus, x1+x2+⋯+xn≤nx_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}\leq n is the inequality which corresponds to the root of τ\tau. It was verified in [8, Section 1] that 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} is an nn-dimensional lattice polytope (all vertices of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} belong to ℕn{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) which is simple (every vertex is an endpoint of exactly nn edges of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}).

Chapoton [8] formulated a number of intriguing conjectures on the lattice point enumeration of arbor polytopes. The first of these concerns the vector h⁡(τ)=(hi​(τ))0≤i≤nh(\tau)=(h_{i}(\tau))_{0\leq i\leq n}, where hi​(τ)h_{i}(\tau) is the number of points in 𝒬τ∩ℕn{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau}\cap{\mathbb{N}}^{n} which have exactly ii nonzero coordinates.

Conjecture 1.1.

([8, Conjecture 0.1]) The vector h⁡(τ)h(\tau) is equal to the hh-vector of an nn-dimensional simplicial polytope for every arbor τ\tau of size nn. In particular, h⁡(τ)h(\tau) is palindromic and unimodal.

The palindromicity of h⁡(τ)h(\tau) (meaning, the statement that hi​(τ)=hn−i​(τ)h_{i}(\tau)=h_{n-i}(\tau) for 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n) is by itself nontrivial. It would imply that the generating polynomial h⁡(τ,t)=∑i=0nhi​(τ)​tih(\tau,t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}h_{i}(\tau)t^{i} of h⁡(τ)h(\tau) can be written uniquely in the form

(2) h⁡(τ,t)=∑i=0⌊n/2⌋γi​(τ)​ti​(1+t)n−2​ih(\tau,t)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\gamma_{i}(\tau)t^{i}(1+t)^{n-2i}

for some integers γ0​(τ),γ1​(τ)​…,γ⌊n/2⌋​(τ)\gamma_{0}(\tau),\gamma_{1}(\tau)\dots,\gamma_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}(\tau). The nonnegativity of these numbers, known as γ\gamma-positivity (see [1] for a survey of this important notion), is stronger than the palindromicity and unimodality of h⁡(τ,t)h(\tau,t). The γ\gamma-positivity of h⁡(τ,t)h(\tau,t) was implicitly conjectured in [8, Section 0.1] as well.

The second main conjecture of [8] concerns the Ehrhart polynomials of arbor polytopes. We recall from [15, Section 4.6] (see also [9] and references therein) that the Ehrhart polynomial of a lattice polytope 𝒬⊂ℝ≥0n{\mathcal{Q}}\subset{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n} is the unique polynomial Ehr⁡(𝒬,t){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},t) with the property that Ehr⁡(𝒬,m)=#⁡(m​𝒬∩ℕn){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},m)=\#(m{\mathcal{Q}}\cap{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) for every m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}. The h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial h∗​(𝒬,t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}},t) of 𝒬{\mathcal{Q}} is defined by the equation

(3) ∑m≥0Ehr⁡(𝒬,m)​tm=h∗​(𝒬,t)(1−t)d+1,\sum_{m\geq 0}{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},m)t^{m}=\frac{h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}},t)}{(1-t)^{d+1}},

where d=dim(𝒬)d=\dim({\mathcal{Q}}). The h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial always has nonnegative coefficients, a property which may fail for the Ehrhart polynomial; see, for instance, [9, Section 4]. An old theorem of Brenti [7, Theorem 4.4.4] implies that if all roots of Ehr⁡(𝒬,t){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},t) are real and lie in the interval [−1,0][-1,0], then all roots of h∗​(𝒬,t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}},t) are real as well.

Conjecture 1.2.

([8, Conjecture 2.2]) For every arbor τ\tau, all roots of the Ehrhart polynomial of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} are real and lie in the interval [−1,0][-1,0]. In particular, the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} has only real roots.

The real-rootedness of h∗​(𝒬τ,t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t) is implied by a weaker property of the Ehrhart polynomial. One may express this polynomial as

(4) n!​Ehr​(𝒬τ,t)=∑i=0nci​(τ)​ti​(1+t)n−in!\,{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}c_{i}(\tau)t^{i}(1+t)^{n-i}

for some integers c0​(τ),c1​(τ),…,cn​(τ)c_{0}(\tau),c_{1}(\tau),\dots,c_{n}(\tau). Following [9], we call Ehr⁡(𝒬τ,t){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t) magic positive if these integers are nonnegative. A theorem of Brändén [6, Theorem 4.2] implies in this situation that h∗​(𝒬τ,t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t) has only real roots. Thus, one may attempt to prove the real-rootedness of the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial of 𝒬τ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau} by providing a combinatorial interpretation of these integers.

Conjecture 1.1 and the γ\gamma-positivity of h⁡(τ,t)h(\tau,t) were verified in the special case of linear arbors in [2]. The aim of this paper is to address these questions for the polytopes 𝒬n,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k}. This polytope is simply the arbor polytope associated to the arbor τn,k\tau_{n,k} which has the (n−k)(n-k)-element set {k+1,k+2,…,n}\{k+1,k+2,\dots,n\} as its root and the singletons {i}\{i\} for i∈[k]i\in[k] as the leaves of the root (one may call such an arbor an octopus). Here are two of our main results for 𝒬n,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k}.

Theorem 1.3.

The polynomial h⁡(τn,k,t)h(\tau_{n,k},t) is γ\gamma-positive and, in particular, palindromic and unimodal, for all n,kn,k.

Theorem 1.4.

We have

(5) n!​Ehr​(𝒬n,k,t)=∑i=0nci​ti​(1+t)n−in!\,{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k},t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}c_{i}t^{i}(1+t)^{n-i}

for some nonnegative integers c0,c1,…,cnc_{0},c_{1},\dots,c_{n}. In particular, the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial of 𝒬n,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k} has only real roots.

Our third main result for 𝒬n,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k} is an explicit combinatorial interpretation of its h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial. The sum of the coefficients of this polynomial is known to equal the normalized volume of 𝒬n,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k} (defined as the volume of 𝒬n,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k} multiplied by n!n!). One can easily verify (for example, as a consequence of Equation (8) in Section 3) that the normalized volume of 𝒬n,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k} is equal to the number of maps f:[n]→[n]f:[n]\rightarrow[n] which contain the set [k][k] in their image (this is a reason to expect apriori that 𝒬n,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k} may have interesting lattice point enumerative properties). The following statement is a natural refinement of this observation. We recall that des⁡(w){\rm des}(w) denotes the number of descents of a word w=(w1,w2,…,wn)∈[n]nw=(w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{n})\in[n]^{n}, meaning indices i∈[n−1]i\in[n-1] such that wi>wi+1w_{i}>w_{i+1}.

Theorem 1.5.

We have

(6) h∗​(𝒬n,k,t)=∑w∈𝒲n,ktn−1−des⁡(w),h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k},t)=\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{W}}_{n,k}}t^{n-1-{\rm des}(w)},

where 𝒲n,k{\mathcal{W}}_{n,k} is the set of words w∈[n]nw\in[n]^{n} in which each of 1,2,…,k1,2,\dots,k appears at least once.

In particular, the right-hand side of (6) has only real roots for all n,kn,k.

Theorem 1.3 is proven in Section 2 by means of an explicit combinatorial formula (see Proposition 2.2) for the coefficients γi​(τn,k)\gamma_{i}(\tau_{n,k}) of Equation (2). Theorems 1.4 and 1.5 are proven in Sections 3 and 4, respectively. To prove Theorem 1.4, a combinatorial interpretation of the coefficients cic_{i} of Equation (5) is provided in terms of a new parking model for cars. The motivation behind this proof comes from [4], where a similar result is proven for Pitman-Stanley polytopes with positive integer parameters. Some generalizations, including a conjectural generalization of Theorem 1.5 to all arbor polytopes, are discussed in Section 5.

Throughout this paper, we use the notation ℕ={0,1,2,…}{\mathbb{N}}=\{0,1,2,\dots\} and [n]={1,2,…,n}[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\} for n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and denote by |S||S| the cardinality of a finite set SS. Background on Ehrhart theory can be found in [5, 9, 11] [15, Chapter 4].

2. Gamma-positivity

This section proves Theorem 1.3. That result is a consequence of the explicit formula of Proposition 2.2. The proof is rather computational; we leave the task to find a bijective proof as an interesting open problem.

The following lemma is a direct consequence of the definition of h⁡(τn,k,t)h(\tau_{n,k},t).

Lemma 2.1.

For every positive integer nn and every k∈{0,1,…,n}k\in\{0,1,\dots,n\},

tn​h​(τn,k,1/t)=∑j=0n∑i=0n−k(n−ki)​(kj−i)​(n−k+j−ij)​tj.t^{n}h(\tau_{n,k},1/t)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-k}{n-k\choose i}{k\choose j-i}{n-k+j-i\choose j}t^{j}.
Proof.

The lattice points in 𝒬n,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k} are the vectors x=(x1,x2,…,xn)∈ℕnx=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} which satisfy (1). Given j∈{0,1,…,n}j\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}, we need to show that the number of these vectors which have exactly jj zero coordinates is equal to

∑i=0n−k(n−ki)​(kj−i)​(n−k+j−ij).\sum_{i=0}^{n-k}{n-k\choose i}{k\choose j-i}{n-k+j-i\choose j}.

To enumerate these elements, let ii be the number of zero coordinates among xk+1,…,xnx_{k+1},\dots,x_{n}. There are (n−ki){n-k\choose i} ways to choose these coordinates and (kj−i){k\choose j-i} ways to choose the remaining zero coordinates of xx. The k−j+ik-j+i nonzero coordinates among x1,x2,…,xkx_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k} must all be equal to 1. The remaining n−k−in-k-i nonzero coordinates of xx have sum no larger than n−k+j−in-k+j-i. Thus, they can be chosen in (n−k+j−ij){n-k+j-i\choose j} ways and the proof follows. ∎

Proposition 2.2.

We have

h⁡(τn,k,t)=∑i=0⌊n/2⌋(n−ki)​(n−ii)​ti​(1+t)n−2​ih(\tau_{n,k},t)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}{n-k\choose i}{n-i\choose i}t^{i}(1+t)^{n-2i}

for all n,kn,k. In particular, h⁡(τn,k,t)h(\tau_{n,k},t) is γ\gamma-positive, and hence palindromic and unimodal.

Proof.

By Lemma 2.1 we have

[tn−j]​h​(τn,k,t)=∑i=0n−k(n−ki)​(kj−i)​(n−k+j−ij).[t^{n-j}]h(\tau_{n,k},t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-k}{n-k\choose i}{k\choose j-i}{n-k+j-i\choose j}.

By Vandermonde’s identity,

(n−k+j−ij)=∑r=0n−k−i(n−k−ir)​(jr){n-k+j-i\choose j}=\sum_{r=0}^{n-k-i}{n-k-i\choose r}{j\choose r}

and hence

[tn−j]​h​(τn,k,t)\displaystyle[t^{n-j}]h(\tau_{n,k},t) =∑i=0n−k(n−ki)​(kj−i)​∑r=0n−k−i(n−k−ir)​(jr)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{n-k}{n-k\choose i}{k\choose j-i}\sum_{r=0}^{n-k-i}{n-k-i\choose r}{j\choose r}
=∑r=0n−k(jr)​∑i=0n−k−r(n−ki)​(kj−i)​(n−k−ir).\displaystyle=\sum_{r=0}^{n-k}{j\choose r}\sum_{i=0}^{n-k-r}{n-k\choose i}{k\choose j-i}{n-k-i\choose r}.

We now apply the identity

(n−ki)​(n−k−ir)=(n−kr)​(n−k−ri){n-k\choose i}{n-k-i\choose r}={n-k\choose r}{n-k-r\choose i}

to obtain that

[tn−j]​h​(τn,k,t)\displaystyle[t^{n-j}]h(\tau_{n,k},t) =∑r=0n−k(n−kr)​(jr)​∑i=0n−k−r(n−k−ri)​(kj−i)\displaystyle=\sum_{r=0}^{n-k}{n-k\choose r}{j\choose r}\sum_{i=0}^{n-k-r}{n-k-r\choose i}{k\choose j-i}
=∑r=0n−k(n−kr)​(jr)​(n−rj),\displaystyle=\sum_{r=0}^{n-k}{n-k\choose r}{j\choose r}{n-r\choose j},

where the last equality follows from Vandermonde’s identity. Since

(jr)​(n−rj)=(n−rr)​(n−2​rj−r),{j\choose r}{n-r\choose j}={n-r\choose r}{n-2r\choose j-r},

we conclude that

[tn−j]​h​(τn,k,t)=∑r=0n−k(n−kr)​(n−rr)​(n−2​rj−r).[t^{n-j}]h(\tau_{n,k},t)=\sum_{r=0}^{n-k}{n-k\choose r}{n-r\choose r}{n-2r\choose j-r}.

Thus, we have shown that

tn​h​(τn,k,1/t)\displaystyle t^{n}h(\tau_{n,k},1/t) =∑j=0n∑r=0n−k(n−kr)​(n−rr)​(n−2​rj−r)​tj.\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\sum_{r=0}^{n-k}{n-k\choose r}{n-r\choose r}{n-2r\choose j-r}t^{j}.

Finally, we interchange the order of summation to conclude that

tn​h​(τn,k,1/t)\displaystyle t^{n}h(\tau_{n,k},1/t) =∑r=0n−k(n−kr)​(n−rr)​tr​∑j=0n(n−2​rj−r)​tj−r\displaystyle=\sum_{r=0}^{n-k}{n-k\choose r}{n-r\choose r}t^{r}\sum_{j=0}^{n}{n-2r\choose j-r}t^{j-r}
=∑r=0⌊n/2⌋(n−kr)​(n−rr)​tr​(1+t)n−2​r.\displaystyle=\sum_{r=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}{n-k\choose r}{n-r\choose r}t^{r}(1+t)^{n-2r}.

This expression is equivalent to the proposed identity. ∎

Remark 2.3.

The polynomial h⁡(τn,k,t)h(\tau_{n,k},t) is in fact real-rooted. Indeed, by [10, Remark 3.1.1], this statement is equivalent to the real-rootedness of

γ⁡(τn,k,t):=∑i=0⌊n/2⌋(n−ki)​(n−ii)​ti.\gamma(\tau_{n,k},t):=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}{n-k\choose i}{n-i\choose i}t^{i}.

Clearly,

pn,k​(t):=∑i=0n−k(n−ki)​ti=(1+t)n−kp_{n,k}(t):=\sum_{i=0}^{n-k}{n-k\choose i}t^{i}=(1+t)^{n-k}

is real-rooted and

qn​(t):=∑i=0⌊n/2⌋(n−ii)​tiq_{n}(t):=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}{n-i\choose i}t^{i}

satisfies the recurrence relation qn​(t)=qn−1​(t)+t​qn−2​(t)q_{n}(t)=q_{n-1}(t)+t\,q_{n-2}(t) and hence is real-rooted by [12, Theorem 1.1]. Therefore, γ⁡(τn,k,t)\gamma(\tau_{n,k},t) is real-rooted as the Hadamard product of pn,k​(t)p_{n,k}(t) and qn​(t)q_{n}(t); see [14, V 155] [16] for Hadamard products of real-rooted polynomials. ∎

3. Magic positivity

This section proves Theorem 1.4. The formulas in the next statement follow from the relevant definitions in a relatively straightforward way.

Proposition 3.1.

For all n,kn,k:

  • (a)
    n!​Ehr​(𝒬n,k,t)=∑j=0k(−1)j​(kj)​∏i=0n−1((n−j)​t+n−j−i).n!\,{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k},t)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}{k\choose j}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}((n-j)t+n-j-i).
  • (b)
    n!​Ehr​(𝒬n,k,t)=∑i=0nci​ti​(1+t)n−i,n!\,{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k},t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}c_{i}t^{i}(1+t)^{n-i},

    where

    (7) ∑j=0k(−1)j​(kj)​∏i=0n−1(i​t+n−j−i)=∑i=0nci​ti.\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}{k\choose j}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(it+n-j-i)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}c_{i}t^{i}.
Proof.

According to the definition of 𝒬n,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k}, Ehr⁡(𝒬n,k,m){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k},m) is equal to the number of points (x1,x2,…,xn)∈ℕn(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} such that

x1+x2+⋯+xn≤m​nx_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}\leq mn, and
xi≤mx_{i}\leq m for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k

for every m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}. Since the number of points (x1,x2,…,xn)∈ℕn(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} which satisfy the first inequality and violate the second for any jj given values of i∈[k]i\in[k] is equal to ((n−j)​(m+1)n)\binom{(n-j)(m+1)}{n}, it follows by inclusion-exclusion that

(8) Ehr⁡(𝒬n,k,m)=∑i=0k(−1)j​(kj)​((n−j)​(m+1)n){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k},m)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}\binom{k}{j}\binom{(n-j)(m+1)}{n}

for every m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}. This proves part (a). Part (b) follows by rewriting the formula of part (a) in the form

n!​Ehr​(𝒬n,k,t)=∑j=0k(−1)j​(kj)​∏i=0n−1(i​t+(n−j−i)​(1+t)).n!\,{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k},t)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}{k\choose j}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(it+(n-j-i)(1+t)).

∎

We need to show that the left-hand side of Equation (7) has nonnegative coefficients; see Table 1 for its value for n≤4n\leq 4. For that reason, we introduce the following variant of the classical parking protocol for cars (see, for instance, [17]). Suppose that nn cars C1,C2,…,CnC_{1},C_{2},\dots,C_{n} want to park on a street with nn parking spaces 1,2,…,n1,2,\dots,n. Any word w=(w1,w2,…,wn)∈[n]nw=(w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{n})\in[n]^{n} may be interpreted as a sequence of parking preferences, where wiw_{i} is the preferred parking space of CiC_{i}. The cars park one at a time in the order C1,C2,…,CnC_{1},C_{2},\dots,C_{n}. Each car CiC_{i} parks in its preferred space wiw_{i}, if available. Otherwise, it parks in the largest available parking space, i.e., it parks in space nn, if available, otherwise in space n−1n-1, if available, and so on. Note that every car parks, under this protocol.

Given w∈[n]nw\in[n]^{n}, we say that a car is lucky if it parks in its preferred parking space and denote by unlucky⁡(w){\rm unlucky}(w) the number of cars which are not lucky. For example, if n=5n=5 and w=(3,5,3,4,1)w=(3,5,3,4,1), then C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} and C5C_{5} are lucky and unlucky⁡(w)=2{\rm unlucky}(w)=2.

Proposition 3.2.

Let

(9) fn,k​(t):=∑j=0k(−1)j​(kj)​∏i=0n−1(i​t+n−j−i).f_{n,k}(t):=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}{k\choose j}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(it+n-j-i).

Then,

(10) fn,k​(t)=∑w∈𝒲n,ktunlucky⁡(w),f_{n,k}(t)=\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{W}}_{n,k}}t^{{\rm unlucky}(w)},

where 𝒲n,k{\mathcal{W}}_{n,k} is the set of words w∈[n]nw\in[n]^{n} in which each of 1,2,…,k1,2,\dots,k appears at least once.

Proof.

We first observe that

fn,k​(1+t)=∑j=0k(−1)j​(kj)​∏i=0n−1(i​t+n−j)f_{n,k}(1+t)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}{k\choose j}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(it+n-j)

and attempt to interpret combinatorially the right-hand side. The j=0j=0 term of the sum may be interpreted as

∏i=0n−1(i​t+n)=∑φ∈ℱntexc⁡(φ),\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(it+n)=\sum_{\varphi\in{\mathcal{F}}_{n}}t^{{\rm exc}(\varphi)},

where ℱn{\mathcal{F}}_{n} is the set of maps φ:[n]→[2​n−1]\varphi:[n]\rightarrow[2n-1] such that φ⁡(i)≤n+i−1\varphi(i)\leq n+i-1 for every i∈[n]i\in[n] and exc⁡(φ){\rm exc}(\varphi) is the number of i∈[n]i\in[n] such that φ⁡(i)>n\varphi(i)>n. More generally, for every j∈{0,1,…,k}j\in\{0,1,\dots,k\} and all 1≤i1<⋯<ij≤k1\leq i_{1}<\cdots<i_{j}\leq k we have

∏i=0n−1(i​t+n−j)=∑φtexc⁡(φ),\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(it+n-j)=\sum_{\varphi}t^{{\rm exc}(\varphi)},

where the sum ranges over all maps φ∈ℱn\varphi\in{\mathcal{F}}_{n} which contain none of i1,…,iji_{1},\dots,i_{j} in their image. Thus, by inclusion-exclusion,

fn,k​(1+t)=∑w∈ℱn,ktexc⁡(φ),f_{n,k}(1+t)=\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{F}}_{n,k}}t^{{\rm exc}(\varphi)},

where ℱn,k{\mathcal{F}}_{n,k} stands for the set of maps φ∈ℱn\varphi\in{\mathcal{F}}_{n} which contain each of 1,2,…,k1,2,\dots,k in their image.

Let gn,k​(t)g_{n,k}(t) denote the right-hand side of Equation (10). To prove that fn,k​(t)=gn,k​(t)f_{n,k}(t)=g_{n,k}(t), we will enumerate the elements of ℱn,k{\mathcal{F}}_{n,k} and 𝒲n,k{\mathcal{W}}_{n,k} with a given set SS of places where 1,2,…,k1,2,\dots,k appear for the first time. By symmetry, we may consider only elements of these sets for which 1,2,…,k1,2,\dots,k appear for the first time in this order. So, let S={s1,s2,…,sk}S=\{s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{k}\} be a kk-element subset of [n][n], where s1<s2<⋯<sks_{1}<s_{2}<\cdots<s_{k}, and let

fn,k​(S,1+t)\displaystyle f_{n,k}(S;1+t) =∑w∈ℱn,k​(S)texc⁡(φ)\displaystyle=\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{F}}_{n,k}(S)}t^{{\rm exc}(\varphi)}
gn,k​(S,t)\displaystyle g_{n,k}(S;t) =∑w∈𝒲n,k​(S)tunlucky⁡(w),\displaystyle=\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{W}}_{n,k}(S)}t^{{\rm unlucky}(w)},

where ℱn,k​(S){\mathcal{F}}_{n,k}(S) stands for the set of maps φ∈ℱn,k\varphi\in{\mathcal{F}}_{n,k} for which sis_{i} is the smallest j∈[n]j\in[n] such that φ⁡(j)=i\varphi(j)=i, for every i∈[k]i\in[k], and similarly, 𝒲n,k​(S){\mathcal{W}}_{n,k}(S) stands for the set of words w∈𝒲n,kw\in{\mathcal{W}}_{n,k} for which sis_{i} is the smallest j∈[n]j\in[n] such that wj=iw_{j}=i, for every i∈[k]i\in[k]. Then,

fn,k​(1+t)\displaystyle f_{n,k}(1+t) =k!​∑Sfn,k​(S,1+t)\displaystyle=k!\sum_{S}f_{n,k}(S;1+t)
gn,k​(t)\displaystyle g_{n,k}(t) =k!​∑Sgn,k​(S,t),\displaystyle=k!\sum_{S}g_{n,k}(S;t),

where the sums range over all kk-element subsets of [n][n]. Hence, it suffices to show that

(11) fn,k​(S,1+t)=gn,k​(S,1+t)f_{n,k}(S;1+t)=g_{n,k}(S;1+t)

for every SS. This will follow from product formulas for fn,k​(S,1+t)f_{n,k}(S;1+t) and gn,k​(S,1+t)g_{n,k}(S;1+t), which are consequences of the multiplication principle. Indeed, let S⊆[n]S\subseteq[n] be as before and set s0:=0s_{0}:=0 and sk+1:=n+1s_{k+1}:=n+1. Given φ∈ℱn,k​(S)\varphi\in{\mathcal{F}}_{n,k}(S) and j∈[n]j\in[n] such that si<j<si+1s_{i}<j<s_{i+1} for some i∈{0,1,…,k}i\in\{0,1,\dots,k\}, there are j−1j-1 possible values for φ⁡(j)\varphi(j) larger than nn and n−k+in-k+i possible values ≤n\leq n, namely the elements of [n][n] other than i+1,i+2,…,ki+1,i+2,\dots,k. Hence

(12) fn,k​(S,1+t)=∏j∈[n]∖Spj​(S,t),f_{n,k}(S;1+t)=\prod_{j\in[n]{\smallsetminus}S}p_{j}(S;t),

where

(13) pj​(S,t)=n−k+i+(j−1)​tp_{j}(S;t)=n-k+i+(j-1)t

for j∈[n]∖Sj\in[n]{\smallsetminus}S with si<j<si+1s_{i}<j<s_{i+1}.

Similarly, let w∈𝒲n,k​(S)w\in{\mathcal{W}}_{n,k}(S) be a word and j∈[n]∖Sj\in[n]{\smallsetminus}S, so that si<j<si+1s_{i}<j<s_{i+1} for some i∈{0,1,…,k}i\in\{0,1,\dots,k\}. We observe that all cars which correspond to elements of SS are lucky. Thus, when car CjC_{j} attempts to park, there are j−1j-1 values of wjw_{j} which make car CjC_{j} unlucky, namely the numbers of the spaces where cars C1,C2,…,Cj−1C_{1},C_{2},\dots,C_{j-1} have parked, and n−k−(j−1−i)n-k-(j-1-i) values of wjw_{j} which make car jj lucky, as many as the spaces among those numbered as k+1,k+2,…,nk+1,k+2,\dots,n which are free at that stage. We conclude that

(14) gn,k​(S,t)=∏j∈[n]∖Sqj​(S,t),g_{n,k}(S;t)=\prod_{j\in[n]{\smallsetminus}S}q_{j}(S;t),

where

(15) qj​(S,t)=n−k+i−j+1+(j−1)​tq_{j}(S;t)=n-k+i-j+1+(j-1)t

for j∈[n]∖Sj\in[n]{\smallsetminus}S with si<j<si+1s_{i}<j<s_{i+1}. We now observe, in view of Equations (13) and (15), that pj​(S,t)=qj​(S,1+t)p_{j}(S;t)=q_{j}(S;1+t) for every j∈[n]∖Sj\in[n]{\smallsetminus}S. Thus, (11) holds by Equations (12) and (14) and the proof follows. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

This follows by combining part (b) of Proposition 3.1 with Proposition 3.2. ∎

4. The h∗h^{*}-polynomial

This section proves Theorem 1.5.

Proof of Theorem 1.5.

By Equation (8),

Ehr⁡(𝒬n,k,m)\displaystyle{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k},m) =∑i=0k(−1)i​(ki)​((n−i)​(m+1)n)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^{i}\binom{k}{i}\binom{(n-i)(m+1)}{n}
=∑i=0k(−1)i​(ki)​[tn]​(1+t)(n−i)​(m+1)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^{i}\binom{k}{i}[t^{n}](1+t)^{(n-i)(m+1)}
=[tn]​∑i=0k(−1)i​(ki)​(1+t)(n−i)​(m+1)\displaystyle=[t^{n}]\sum_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^{i}\binom{k}{i}(1+t)^{(n-i)(m+1)}
=[tn]​(1+t)n⁡(m+1)​∑i=0k(−1)i​(ki)​((1+t)−(m+1))i\displaystyle=[t^{n}](1+t)^{n(m+1)}\sum_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^{i}\binom{k}{i}\bigl((1+t)^{-(m+1)}\bigr)^{i}
=[tn]​(1+t)n⁡(m+1)​(1−(1+t)−(m+1))k\displaystyle=[t^{n}](1+t)^{n(m+1)}\bigl(1-(1+t)^{-(m+1)}\bigr)^{k}
=[tn]​(1+t)(n−k)​(m+1)​((1+t)m+1−1)k.\displaystyle=[t^{n}](1+t)^{(n-k)(m+1)}\bigl((1+t)^{m+1}-1\bigr)^{k}.

We expand the two factors as

((1+t)m+1−1)k=∏i=1k(∑ai=1m+1(m+1ai)​tai),\bigl((1+t)^{m+1}-1\bigr)^{k}=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\Bigl(\sum_{a_{i}=1}^{m+1}\binom{m+1}{a_{i}}t^{a_{i}}\Bigr),
(1+t)(n−k)​(m+1)=∏i=k+1n(∑ai=0m+1(m+1ai)​tai)(1+t)^{(n-k)(m+1)}=\prod_{i=k+1}^{n}\Bigl(\sum_{a_{i}=0}^{m+1}\binom{m+1}{a_{i}}t^{a_{i}}\Bigr)

and extract the coefficient of tnt^{n} to conclude that

(16) Ehr⁡(𝒬n,k,m)=∑a1+⋯+an=na1,…,ak≥1,ak+1,…,an≥0∏i=1n(m+1ai),{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k},m)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{1}+\dots+a_{n}=n\\ a_{1},\dots,a_{k}\geq 1,\;a_{k+1},\dots,a_{n}\geq 0\end{subarray}}\;\prod_{i=1}^{n}\binom{m+1}{a_{i}},

where the sum ranges over all weak compositions μ=(a1,a2,…,an)\mu=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}) of nn such that a1,a2,…,ak≥1a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{k}\geq 1. For such a weak composition μ\mu, we denote by 𝒮μ{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu} the set of all permutations of the multiset containing aia_{i} copies of ii for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. MacMahon’s formula [13, p. 211] states that

∑m≥0(m+a1a1)(m+a2a2)⋯(m+anan)tm=∑w∈𝒮μtdes⁡(w)(1−t)n+1.\sum_{m\geq 0}\binom{m+a_{1}}{a_{1}}\binom{m+a_{2}}{a_{2}}\!\cdots\!\binom{m+a_{n}}{a_{n}}t^{m}=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}}t^{{\rm des}(w)}}{(1-t)^{\,n+1}}.

Since ai>0a_{i}>0 for at least one ii, we may replace mm by −m-m in the coefficient of tmt^{m} on the left-hand side and apply [15, Proposition 4.2.3] to reach the identity

∑m≥0(m+1a1)(m+1a2)⋯(m+1an)tm=∑w∈𝒮μtn−1−des⁡(w)(1−t)n+1.\sum_{m\geq 0}\binom{m+1}{a_{1}}\binom{m+1}{a_{2}}\!\cdots\!\binom{m+1}{a_{n}}t^{m}=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}}t^{\,n-1-{\rm des}(w)}}{(1-t)^{\,n+1}}.

We now sum this identity over all weak compositions μ\mu of nn satisfying the conditions in (16) and observe that the union ⋃μ𝒮μ\bigcup_{\mu}{{\mathcal{S}}_{\mu}}, where μ\mu ranges over these weak compositions, is exactly the set 𝒲n,k{\mathcal{W}}_{n,k}. We conclude that

∑m≥0Ehr⁡(𝒬n,k,m)​tm=∑w∈𝒲n,ktn−1−des⁡(w)(1−t)n+1\sum_{m\geq 0}{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k},m)\,t^{m}=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{W}}_{n,k}}t^{\,n-1-{\rm des}(w)}}{(1-t)^{n+1}}

and the proof follows. ∎

5. Generalizations

A natural generalization of 𝒬n,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,k} is the lattice polytope 𝒬n,d,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,d,k} in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} defined by the inequalities

xi≥0x_{i}\geq 0 for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n,
xi≤1x_{i}\leq 1 for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, and
x1+x2+⋯+xn≤dx_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}\leq d,

where n,dn,d are positive integers and k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}} is such that k≤min⁡{n,d}k\leq\min\{n,d\}. A nice feature of this polytope is that its normalized volume is equal to the number of maps f:[n]→[d]f:[n]\rightarrow[d] which contain 1,2,…,k1,2,\dots,k in their image. This follows by computing the coefficient of tn/n!t^{n}/n! in the expression

(17) Ehr⁡(𝒬n,d,k,t)=∑i=0k(−1)j​(kj)​((d−j)​t+n−jn),{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{n,d,k},t)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}\binom{k}{j}\binom{(d-j)t+n-j}{n},

which directly generalizes Equation (8).

One can easily find examples of polytopes 𝒬n,d,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,d,k} with d<nd<n (such as the 3-dimensional simplex 𝒬3,2,0{\mathcal{Q}}_{3,2,0}) for which the Ehrhart polynomial is not magic positive. The following generalization of Theorem 1.4 gives a positive result for d≥nd\geq n. We sketch the proof, which directly extends that of Theorem 1.4. The main difference is in the parking protocol used, where parking preferences now are words w=(w1,w2,…,wn)∈[d]nw=(w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{n})\in[d]^{n} (there are again nn cars C1,C2,…,CnC_{1},C_{2},\dots,C_{n} and nn parking spaces 1,2,…,n1,2,\dots,n). Every preference wi>nw_{i}>n is considered unavailable and thus, car CiC_{i} parks in the largest available space.

Theorem 5.1.

The Ehrhart polynomial of 𝒬n,d,k{\mathcal{Q}}_{n,d,k} is magic positive whenever d≥nd\geq n. More precisely, we have

n!​Ehr​(𝒬n,d,k,t)=∑i=0nci​ti​(1+t)n−i,n!\,{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{n,d,k},t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}c_{i}t^{i}(1+t)^{n-i},

where

(18) ∑i=0nci​ti=∑w∈𝒲n,d,ktunlucky⁡(w)\sum_{i=0}^{n}c_{i}t^{i}=\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{W}}_{n,d,k}}t^{{\rm unlucky}(w)}

and 𝒲n,d,k{\mathcal{W}}_{n,d,k} is the set of words w∈[d]nw\in[d]^{n} in which each of 1,2,…,k1,2,\dots,k appears at least once.

Proof.

We may rewrite Equation (17) as

n!​Ehr​(𝒬n,d,k,t)\displaystyle n!\,{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{n,d,k},t) =∑j=0k(−1)j​(kj)​∏i=0n−1((d−j)​t+n−j−i)\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}{k\choose j}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}((d-j)t+n-j-i)
=∑i=0nci​ti​(1+t)n−i,\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{n}c_{i}t^{i}(1+t)^{n-i},

where

(19) ∑j=0k(−1)j​(kj)​∏i=0n−1((d−n+i)​t+n−j−i)=∑i=0nci​ti.\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}{k\choose j}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}((d-n+i)t+n-j-i)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}c_{i}t^{i}.

Let us denote the left-hand side of Equation (19) by fn,d,k​(t)f_{n,d,k}(t) and the right-hand side of Equation (18) by gn,d,k​(t)g_{n,d,k}(t). We need to show that fn,d,k​(t)=gn,d,k​(t)f_{n,d,k}(t)=g_{n,d,k}(t). We note that

fn,d,k​(1+t)=∑j=0k(−1)j​(kj)​∏i=0n−1((d−n+i)​t+d−j)f_{n,d,k}(1+t)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{j}{k\choose j}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}((d-n+i)t+d-j)

and interpret the j=0j=0 term of this sum as

∏i=0n−1((d−n+i)​t+d)=∑φ∈ℱn,d,0texc⁡(φ),\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}((d-n+i)t+d)=\sum_{\varphi\in{\mathcal{F}}_{n,d,0}}t^{{\rm exc}(\varphi)},

where ℱn,d,0{\mathcal{F}}_{n,d,0} is the set of maps φ:[n]→[2​d−1]\varphi:[n]\rightarrow[2d-1] such that φ⁡(i)≤2​d−n+i−1\varphi(i)\leq 2d-n+i-1 for every i∈[n]i\in[n] and exc⁡(φ){\rm exc}(\varphi) is the number of i∈[n]i\in[n] such that φ⁡(i)>d\varphi(i)>d. As in the proof of Proposition 3.2, we deduce by inclusion-exclusion that

fn,d,k​(1+t)=∑w∈ℱn,d,ktexc⁡(φ),f_{n,d,k}(1+t)=\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{F}}_{n,d,k}}t^{{\rm exc}(\varphi)},

where ℱn,d,k{\mathcal{F}}_{n,d,k} is the set of maps φ∈ℱn,d,0\varphi\in{\mathcal{F}}_{n,d,0} which contain each of 1,2,…,k1,2,\dots,k in their image. For S={s1,s2,…,sk}⊆[n]S=\{s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{k}\}\subseteq[n] with s1<s2<⋯<sks_{1}<s_{2}<\cdots<s_{k}, we let

fn,d,k​(S,1+t)\displaystyle f_{n,d,k}(S;1+t) =∑w∈ℱn,d,k​(S)texc⁡(φ)\displaystyle=\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{F}}_{n,d,k}(S)}t^{{\rm exc}(\varphi)}
gn,d,k​(S,t)\displaystyle g_{n,d,k}(S;t) =∑w∈𝒲n,d,k​(S)tunlucky⁡(w),\displaystyle=\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{W}}_{n,d,k}(S)}t^{{\rm unlucky}(w)},

where ℱn,d,k​(S){\mathcal{F}}_{n,d,k}(S) is the set of maps φ∈ℱn,d,k\varphi\in{\mathcal{F}}_{n,d,k} for which sis_{i} is the smallest j∈[n]j\in[n] such that φ⁡(j)=i\varphi(j)=i, for every i∈[k]i\in[k], and similarly, 𝒲n,d,k​(S){\mathcal{W}}_{n,d,k}(S) is the set of words w∈𝒲n,d,kw\in{\mathcal{W}}_{n,d,k} for which sis_{i} is the smallest j∈[n]j\in[n] such that wj=iw_{j}=i, for every i∈[k]i\in[k]. Then, it suffices to show that fn,d,k​(S,1+t)=gn,d,k​(S,1+t)f_{n,d,k}(S;1+t)=g_{n,d,k}(S;1+t) for every SS and the proof of Proposition 3.2 works, with the modified formulas

pj​(S,t)=d−k+i+(d−n+j−1)​tp_{j}(S;t)=d-k+i+(d-n+j-1)t

and

qj​(S,t)=n−k+i−j+1+(d−n+j−1)​tq_{j}(S;t)=n-k+i-j+1+(d-n+j-1)t

for j∈[n]∖Sj\in[n]{\smallsetminus}S with si<j<si+1s_{i}<j<s_{i+1}; the details are omitted. ∎

We conclude with a conjectural generalization of Theorem 1.5 for every arbor τ\tau. We recall that the set 𝒟⁡(v){\mathcal{D}}(v) is defined in the introduction for all vertices vv of τ\tau. Extensive experimentation by computer supports the following conjecture.

Conjecture 5.2.

For every arbor τ\tau of size nn

h∗​(𝒬τ,t)=∑w∈𝒲τtn−1−des⁡(w),h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\tau},t)=\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{W}}_{\tau}}t^{n-1-{\rm des}(w)},

where 𝒲τ{\mathcal{W}}_{\tau} is the set of words w∈[n]nw\in[n]^{n} with the following property: for every vertex vv of τ\tau, the elements of 𝒟⁡(v){\mathcal{D}}(v) appear a total of at least |𝒟⁡(v)||{\mathcal{D}}(v)| times in ww.

The validity of this statement is unclear even for linear arbors, studied in [2]. An even more general conjecture will appear in [3].
